doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: Sound, Kenny G and smooth jazz
title: Smooth jazz, Kenny G and stealing from Grover Washington
summary: He objects to non-jazz people appropriating the jazz tradition, tells an elevator anecdote about Kenny G, and says Kenny G took his sound from Grover Washington; Duke said good composers borrow, the best steal.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah I noticed something on your website. You said, “Where the jazz in smooth jazz?”

Yeah, well, don’t get me started on that because the smooth jazz — see jazz is a big tent. And there’s nothing wrong with jazz being a big tent. I don’t have a problem with that. The problem I have is when the non-jazz people try to take jazz — not only the term but try to usurp the tradition to make the tradition appear as if it actually sprung from this little popcorn stuff that they’re into. That has nothing to do with art, it just has to do with entertainment, it has also to do with a commercial kind of marketing approach, in other words a post-twentieth century kind of approach to entertainment as opposed to art. And so then when people in education are trying to study this, unless you’re very clear- minded about it and you design your programs in a clear-minded way, it’s very easy for people including musicians to be confused as to what is entertainment, what is art, what are the histories of these various things, the pulls that are involved. I was in the elevator today, this morning. It was really funny. There were some young musicians, high school or maybe younger university students, you know like freshmen or sophomores. And one guy was saying to the other guy, yeah I was just standing in the elevator, and the guy says, “Oh man, that Kenny G, that’s one of the saddest musicians. Boy the guy can play saxophone, he really can, but my parents have the Christmas album, you know, they played that when I was home, man that is horrible.” The kid says, “Really?” “Oh it’s terrible, you wouldn’t believe how it sucks.” I said now this is young guys. Nobody’s putting anything down their gullets or anything. And this guy is telling his friend, like man this stuff sucks man, what is this? And he didn’t even say Bird or Trane or anything, he just said, “Man this is horrible music, just terrible.” And of course on the other hand it’s a white cat too. A white kid. And on the other hand I’ll show you black folks that — I’ll take you to some places and introduce you to some people, say, “Tell me, how do you feel about Kenny G?” And they’ll say, “Oh Kenny G is so wonderful, oh his music is so stirring to me.” [whistles]. But he does have a sound. He does have a sound.
He’s got some formula that apparently appeals to some people.

That he took from Grover Washington of course. I mean Grover is the one that really is the inspiration for Kenny G. If he would just say that, that would make me, then I would get off my high horse. I mean really say well the boy, no matter what he’s doing at least he’s honest about where he’s stealing it from. I mean Duke Ellington would tell you in a minute, “Yeah I stole that from Tchaikovsky, and I took that from Fats Waller and I took this— and I just heard this somewhere, I probably stole it from somewhere but I don’t
know where he got it from.” But you know, as Duke used to say, good composers borrow, the best composers steal. The way it is.
